items.title: Show HN: Zeus – Claude Code for AI voice agents
items.description:
Show HN: Hi everyone, Alex here - I’m one of the founders of ThunderPhone. We’re excited to announce the launch of Zeus, a platform that makes AI phone calls actually work without extensive hand-tuning! You can see a head-to-head I made of the last version of ThunderPhone vs this one here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YlkIc3L29lo A (somewhat long) summary: When we started building business phone agents in 2024, we kept running into technical problems that ruined calls, caused by the limits of existing architectures. The two biggest issues were that phone agents misheard callers, and disobeyed scripts or responded in weird ways. Both stemmed from the prevailing voice agent architecture - a “three-step” or “cascaded” pipeline: one transcription model turning caller audio into text, one LLM generating a response (and sometimes tool calls) from that text, and a TTS model turning response text into audio. Transcription models aren’t perfect, especially in noisy environments, with unclear callers, in languages other than English, and on short utterances like “yeah”. With the pipeline approach, when caller audio is boiled down to a single “best guess” text transcript, mistakes are often unrecoverable: there’s typically no “top n” best guesses or other audio signal for the LLM to use if the transcript was wrong. That leads the LLM to respond to what the transcription model thought it heard instead of what the caller actually said. The pipeline approach also caused weird responses and poor instruction-following due to the tradeoff between LLM speed and intelligence. Phone calls demand fast responses to feel natural, which is in tension with an LLM’s need to “think” and run inference - often for several seconds - to answer many prompts correctly. With a single LLM in the pipeline, the obvious choice is picking one fast enough to feel responsive, but that comes with an unavoidably high error rate on real calls, frustrating callers and sending calls off the rails. More recently, end-to-end “speech-to-speech” models have won usage alongside three-step pipelines. They’re better at hearing callers correctly (though still not perfect), but they’re even worse at following instructions reliably, which is typically disastrous for business phone calls. Once we understood these problems, we built our own stack to address them. Over the past year and a half, the ThunderPhone stack has largely solved mishearing and misbehaving by combining numerous models on each call. For audio misun

items.title: Show HN: erXos – a microkernel OS in Erlang based on Genera/Plan 9/QNX ideas
items.description:
Show HN: What if every Erlang process were an operating-system process? With as much system code and drivers written in Erlang itself. This is something I was pondering for a while, and finally was able to prototype thanks to AI coding agents. erXos is a capability-based microkernel OS in Erlang: drivers, filesystems, and the network stack are all supervised Erlang processes, same as any app. The kernel itself is Fiasco, in C++, slightly modified for erXos needs. This is an OS I wanted for a long time: an Erlang machine where every BEAM process is a process visible to the OS and scheduler, not something bolted on top. You can try it right now with nothing to install: there is an emulator on the website that boots the whole OS in the browser ARM64 emulator. At the rc prompt, try `ps`, `top`, `ping` or `erl` and write any kind of erlang code. There's a Pi 4 SD image and a QEMU image too. The goal is to build an ultra-reliable microkernel OS with hot code loading and both system and BEAM-based isolation. The latter is one thing that would allow you to run millions of processes on the system, something that would be prohibitive on a microkernel alone due to the context switch overhead. Capabilities keep every component least-privileged, supervision keeps the machine running when drivers or subsystems crash, and hot code loading would let you fix a broken driver without reboot. The secondary goal is to keep as much of a UNIX face as possible. Too many novel OSes change things for no particular reason that makes them hard to use. erXos tries to preserve as many existing UNIX/FreeBSD concepts as much as possible to remove the learning curve. What works today: - Boots in the browser/v64, in QEMU, and on a Raspberry Pi 4 from an SD card - A real shell (plan9 rc) with job control, pipes, `ps`, `grep`. It feels like UNIX on the surface - Erlang versions of basic UNIX apps. - Drivers written in Erlang: UART, virtio, SD card, Ethernet (GENET), display - A pure Erlang EROFS filesystem for root images - A TCP/IP stack in Erlang based on FreeBSD network stack and verified for correctness against it - Domains: every app runs as its own address space or Erlang node, isolated from others - Plan 9 namespaces and 9P everywhere; windows are files like RIO and 9P is a file protocol between OS servers - Supervision end to end: if a driver fails, its supervisor resets the device and restarts it I also have 2 demo apps built on app sdk: a full-screen kiosk app with live crypto quotes and cl
Website metadata: erXos is an Erlang-native operating system on a capability microkernel. Every Erlang process is an operating-system process.
items.product_description: erXos is an Erlang-native operating system on a capability microkernel. Every Erlang process is an operating-system process.

items.title: Show HN: Openspot – macOS launcher for disposable tools
items.description:
Show HN: Hi HN! We're Tony, Kolom and Anastasiia, a small team from Ukraine. Today we are open-sourcing Openspot, our research project on using generative UI in day-to-day work. The idea is simple: generate a tool (spot) for your current task using coding agent, and keep it if you like it or remove it after use if you don't. We are using Openspot daily and really enjoying the possibilities it unlocks. Some examples of spots: - caffeinate, which allows the Mac to work with the lid closed - local file and screenshot search in natural language using EmbeddingGemma 2 - draw on screen during calls or before screenshots - AI agents monitoring - AirDrop, but over the network (using iroh) We built it because of two things: 1. Over the past year, we (and almost every designer and engineer we know) have started making small tools using coding agents. But the DX for macOS applications is very frustrating even for coders, and you have to pay for a developer account to share them. 2. And we kind of miss the days of custom Winamp skins and Twitter clients. That's why every part of Openspot is customizable, so anyone can give it their own look and feel. This is a very early stage. The code is MIT-licensed, and the core will remain free forever. We're sticking to macOS 26+ for now (because of Liquid Glass). Ask us anything, or roast it. Any feedback is very appreciated.
Website metadata: Lightweight macOS launcher, extensible by coding agents - celishq/openspot

items.title: Show HN: Purple Flow – AI-first n8n alternative, 10k+ workflows on 512MB
items.description:
Show HN: Hey all! I ran into a wall with n8n - hard and expensive to scale, limited streaming, heavy MCP is confusing for agents. That scaling was becoming more and more critical as I was beginning to build agentic swarms. So I built my own alternative with Elixir and Beam. Been using it in production for almost 2 months. It connects my agent to multiple databases, sandboxes, and APIs. I've even migrated over my most used n8n workflows without a hiccup. I ran some benchmarks and 10,000 concurrent workflows executed in 3 seconds and cost about 330MB of ram (listed as 512 in the case study). Equivalent workflows in n8n took 2GB of ram to run 100. It's roughly 200x the memory efficiency of the usual Node/Python stacks. And while you don't edit the workflows yourself visually, you can see and manage them through a UI, along with credentials that the agent never sees. The workflows themselves are pure TOML. Not as easy as dragging node connectors. But the idea is that AI creates the flows and you can easily understand them. This isn't a shaky demo. I'm using it as my daily driver to create complex multi-agent personas, run research and info gathering swarms, and whatever else my agent needs to get its job done. (it's built more than 70 so far) I have a live working demo on my website that was built by an agent using Purple Flow to connect to my server. The demo itself lets an agent using Purple Flow access live (Adventure Works) data and generate reports, documents, and slides on demand. My agent and I built it in an afternoon. It runs on a lightweight model (to save money for a public demo) with very few hiccups. - Repo: https://github.com/leetheguy/purple_flow - Discord, benchmarks, and demo links in the repo.

items.title: Show HN: Foolscap – a writing app that reads your book and never writes for you
items.description:
Show HN: People are scared of their ability to write and think atrophying, so I wondered: what if I built something that enhanced human creativity instead of destroying it by doing the thinking and writing for people? Foolscap is the result, or at least the first version of that idea that's fleshed out enough to share here. It reads as you write and picks out the structure: characters, ideas, threads, what's left hanging. You can respond to what it picks out, so there's a dialectic between the system and you as the writer. There's also an agent on the side, plugged into the same system, so you can ask about your book and fire off actions through conversation. It never writes into your work. The system can also follow theorems and proofs and string together their dependencies, but I haven't made that a focus yet. There's no Lean support, for example. If anyone's interested in that, I'd love to hear it. I want to build this by iterating with the people who use it: a tool that uses AI not to bypass the creative process, but to bring new tools to it. There's a free tier, and if you email [email removed] I'll send you a code for 50% off. This is my first product, so feedback of any kind is welcome. Thanks, David
Website metadata: Foolscap uses AI to help you write, without writing for you. Foolscap does not generate text for you. Your writing is entirely yours.

items.title: Show HN: Try Vibe Robotics! (IRL or MuJoCo SIM)
items.description:
Show HN: Hey HN, I'm Salman, a research engineer at GDM Robotics on the team that built this robotics plugin. Whether you're a robotics founder, data company, making RL environments, or just getting FOMO seeing all the cool robotics demos on X, you can just plug in a robot and start prompting away. The plugin we've written up includes skills that steer the model toward following best practices. The benefits of using the plugin are: - fewer tokens (and therefore thinking time) needed to do bring-up the robot and to reach a successful attempt on your task - higher fidelity real-to-sim-to-real when creating MuJoCo assets and environments - leveraging strong motion planning, visual servoing, and collision avoidance We have tested on SO-101, YAM, and Franka Duo, but you don't even need real arms to test it out. You can just create cool environments in sim and then prompt the model to control a simulated robot in the environment! (Just make sure to tell it not to use privileged sim state if you want to actually evaluate how good the perception and model intelligence is). Just point your agent to the repo, good luck, and happy tinkering! Let me know if you have any questions! Will answer anything here or feel free to post on the GitHub repo directly.

items.title: Show HN: Robotics needs better CAD, so I wrote a B-rep kernel and 3,487 tests
items.description:
Show HN: Hey HN, I’m Tony. I’m a co-founder of Springcraft, where we have been doing a lot of CAD modeling for robot parts. Our team kept running into limitations with existing kernels, and so I decided to write a new B-rep kernel and a new comprehensive, kernel-agnostic B-rep conformance test suite. Both are available today under MIT licenses. The kernel, springrep, is written in safe Rust with no dependencies. It covers a broad range of our mechanical CAD needs, including advanced fillets, sweeps, lofts, shells, offsets, STEP and exact measurements and queries. Claude Code made it feasible to write this, but it took a lot of time and care to get it right. The test suite, brep-conformance, has 3,487 cases covering the modeling operations common across kernels: booleans, fillets, chamfers, shells, offsets, sweeps, lofts, STEP, and queries with expected answers coming from closed forms and exact geometry. It caught hundreds of bugs, edge cases, and hot spots in springrep that our own tests had missed, and now springrep passes all of it. We’ve also run it on a few popular open-source kernels and anyone can run it on theirs. This is the first version, so there are surely mistakes in the test and adapters. Corrections, pull requests, and new kernels are welcome. kernel: https://github.com/springcraft-ai/springrep conformance suite: https://springcraft-ai.github.io/brep-conformance/
Website metadata: An open-source B-rep geometry kernel in safe Rust with zero dependencies, covering booleans, fillets, sweeps, STEP, and exact measurement. MIT licensed.

items.description:
Show HN: We recently moved our observability stack from DataDog to a self-hosted SigNoz instance to retain Canadian data residency. It's been incredible thus far, big cost savings and a more targeted UI. One downside was that the web UI for SigNoz isn't responsive at all. I ended up building this mobile app. Obviously I'm biased but I think it's much better than the DataDog app, making it easy to keep an eye on things and do light debugging from my phone. I'm not affiliated with SigNoz in any way, but their platform deserves a ton of props
